system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

Here are examples of what I expect:

--- Example 1 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Michael Smith | Age/Sex: 32/M | Admission: 02/03/2026 | Discharge: 05/03/2026
C/O: Loose stools, vomiting, and abdominal cramps for 3 days.
History: Multiple episodes of watery diarrhea with nausea, repeated vomiting, generalised weakness, and abdominal cramps. No blood in stools. No recent travel.
Past History: Hypothyroidism (2 years).
Examination: Temp 99.8°F | Pulse 112 bpm | BP 100/70 mmHg | RR 20/min | SpO₂ 98%.
Investigations: CBC — mild leukocytosis. Serum Electrolytes — hyponatremia. Stool — no blood/parasites. RFT — mildly elevated creatinine due to dehydration.

Output:
Michael Smith, a 32-year-old man, was admitted on 02/03/2026 and discharged on 05/03/2026. He came with 3 days of loose motions (watery diarrhea), vomiting, stomach cramps, and weakness. He has had hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) for 2 years. On arrival, his temperature was 99.8°F (mild fever), pulse was 112 bpm (fast heart rate; normal is 60–100), blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg (borderline low; normal is 120/80), respiratory rate was 20/min, and oxygen was normal at 98%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (mild rise in infection-fighting cells) and hyponatremia (low salt/sodium levels due to fluid loss). Stool tests showed no blood or parasites. Kidney tests showed mildly raised creatinine due to dehydration (lack of fluids). He was treated with IV fluids and supportive medicines, improved well, and was safely discharged home.

--- Example 2 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Robert Brown | Age/Sex: 58/M | Admission: 25/03/2026 | Discharge: 30/03/2026
C/O: Chest pain and sweating for 6 hours.
History: Sudden onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating, mild breathlessness.
Past History: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (8 years). Hypertension (10 years). Dyslipidemia.
Examination: Temp 98.4°F | Pulse 96 bpm | BP 160/100 mmHg | RR 22/min | SpO₂ 95%.
Investigations: ECG — ST depression in anterior leads. Troponin-I — elevated. 2D Echo — mild left ventricular dysfunction. Lipid Profile — elevated LDL cholesterol.

Output:
Robert Brown, a 58-year-old man, was admitted on 25/03/2026 and discharged on 30/03/2026. He has an 8-year history of diabetes (sugar), 10-year hypertension (high BP), and dyslipidemia (high blood cholesterol). He arrived with 6 hours of sudden central chest pain spreading to his left arm, sweating, and mild breathlessness. His temperature was 98.4°F (normal), pulse was 96 bpm, blood pressure was high at 160/100 mmHg (normal 120/80), and oxygen saturation was 95% (borderline). An ECG and elevated troponin-I (a heart damage marker) confirmed a mild heart attack. A 2D Echo (heart ultrasound scan) showed mild left ventricular dysfunction (mild pumping weakness of the heart), and tests showed elevated bad LDL cholesterol. He was stabilized on heart medications and blood thinners, recovered safely, and was discharged home.

output_text:
Your family member was admitted on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours.

He came to the hospital for a hemodialysis (blood filtering machine for kidney failure) session with severe left lower back pain that had started 3 days ago, along with weakness and difficulty walking. The person accompanying him said he did not have fever, nausea, or vomiting. The catheter (a tube for dialysis) dressing in his right thigh vein was leaking.

During his hospital stay, he was diagnosed with several serious infections. He had a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of bacteria resistant to some antibiotics). This infection led to spondylodiscitis (infection of the spinal bones and discs) in his L2-L4 region (lower back), infective endocarditis (infection of the heart valve) in his mitral valve (one of the heart's main valves), and an ileopsoas muscle abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle near the hip) on the left side.

The catheter in his right thigh vein was removed on 11/08, and he was started on antibiotic therapy (treatment with medicines to fight infection) with vancomycin (a strong antibiotic) on the same day, based on culture (lab test to identify bacteria) results. An attempt to drain the abscess in his psoas muscle (a deep muscle in the abdomen) on 12/02 was not successful because bowel loops (parts of the intestine) were in the way.

He showed improvement in the infections in his spine with conservative treatment (treatment without surgery). He remained without fever, and his blood cultures (blood tests for infection) became negative repeatedly. As a complication of being immobile (not moving much), he developed a sacral pressure injury (a bed sore on the lower back), which was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local care. Instructions for caring for this injury at home were given to the team.

He continued to need hemodialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays because of a problem with his arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein for dialysis) in his left arm, where there was some narrowing. He is currently on renal replacement therapy (treatment for kidney failure, like dialysis).

His general condition is good. He is a bit pale, hydrated (has enough fluids), not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), not feverish to the touch, and breathing normally (eupneic) in room air. Neurologically, he is conscious and knows where he is, what time it is, and who he is. When listening to his chest, there were normal breathing sounds with some mild crackles (small popping sounds) at the bottom of both lungs, but no signs of breathing difficulty. His heart rhythm was irregular, with normal heart sounds and no murmurs (abnormal heart sounds). His abdomen (belly) is slightly bulging, with normal bowel sounds, not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. His hands and feet are warm and have good blood flow. In his left arm, the fistula has a thrill (a vibration felt over the fistula, which is a good sign). In his legs, there is some mild swelling and a skin condition called anterior tibial ochre dermatitis (skin discoloration on the shins).

An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan on 25/10/2020 showed a collection of pus in his left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling and enhancement (brightening on the scan after dye injection).

Culture results showed:
- Catheter tip on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to vancomycin.
- Blood culture on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus.
- Blood culture on 11/11: Staphylococcus aureus resistant to oxacillin (another antibiotic) in 2 samples.
- Blood culture on 11/21: Citrobacter koseri (another type of bacteria) in 1 sample, and Staphylococcus aureus in 1 sample.
- Blood culture on 11/24: Staphylococcus capitis (another type of bacteria).
- Blood cultures on 11/28, 12/01, and 12/02 were negative.

An attempted puncture to drain the abscess on 12/02 was not done because of intestinal loops being in the way. A new MRI report of the pelvis from 12/16 was reviewed.

It has been arranged with {organization} for him to attend hemodialysis at {organization} on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, with transport by stretcher taxi from his home city.

Therefore, he is being discharged with the following pending issues:
- He needs to be given 0.5 grams of vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session. This antibiotic treatment will continue until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after his last negative blood culture.
- His arteriovenous fistula needs assessment. A phlebography (X-ray of veins with dye) of the fistula is recommended to find the site of narrowing, or an ultrasound can be done before the procedure. He has been put on a list for this, and {organization} will contact him to schedule the treatment.
- For the sacral pressure injury, the specialist team has noted that he has an outpatient follow-up appointment on 16/01/2021 for reassessment. Instructions for home care of the injury were provided.
- For cardiology (heart specialist) follow-up to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs), he missed an appointment on 09/09. A new appointment is scheduled for 01/13.
- For motor rehabilitation (therapy to improve movement), an appointment with the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at {organization} was requested on 12/27, and we are awaiting the appointment.
- The nuclear magnetic resonance report of the pelvis from 12/16 needs to be checked.
- His previous chronic medications (long-term medicines) are to be continued.
- He will go to the dialysis room on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.
- He has an appointment at the amyloidosis cardiology outpatient clinic on 01/13.
- He has an appointment at the pressure injury surgery outpatient clinic on 01/16.
